knowledgePoints.name: Start the answer for it
knowledgePoints.teach:
Asking for “JSON only” gets you JSON wrapped in a helpful sentence. Asking more firmly gets you a shorter sentence.

The mechanical fix is to write the beginning of the assistant turn yourself. Claude continues from where you left it, so the preamble never gets a place to exist:

messages = [
    {"role": "user",      "content": "Extract the invoice fields as JSON."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "```json"},        # ← prefill
]

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=M, max_tokens=1024, messages=messages,
    stop_sequences=["```"],                              # ← stop at the fence
)

data = json.loads(resp.content[0].text.strip())

Prefill removes the preamble. The stop sequence removes the trailing commentary.

The same trick constrains code, lists, or CSV — anything whose delimiter is unambiguous.

questions.q: Your invoice-extraction endpoint asks Claude for 'JSON only, no explanation,' but production logs show roughly 30% of responses still open with a sentence like 'Here is the extracted JSON:' before the object, breaking your json.loads() parser. Which pair of changes would most reliably eliminate this preamble?
options: Prefill the assistant turn with an opening ```json fence so the response continues from there, and add a stop_sequence on the closing fence to cut off trailing commentary.
Lower the temperature toward zero and increase max_tokens so the model has more room and less randomness to settle into a clean, fully structured JSON response.
Move the 'JSON only' instruction out of the user turn and into the system prompt, where Claude is expected to treat formatting rules as strictly binding on every turn.
Enable streaming and parse only the first delta chunk returned, since the preamble sentence is assumed to be generated only after the JSON object has already begun.
questions.explain: Prefilling the assistant turn with the fence removes the preamble because Claude continues the turn rather than starting fresh, and the stop sequence trims anything that would follow the JSON. Lowering temperature and adding tokens changes how confidently text is generated but does nothing to stop a preamble sentence from being produced in the first place. Relocating the instruction to the system prompt still leaves compliance probabilistic — the same 'ask nicely' approach from a different slot. And streaming doesn't change generation order: the preamble sentence is produced before the JSON, not after, so parsing only the first chunk would capture the sentence, not the object.

questions.q: A teammate claims that prefilling the assistant turn works by sending a hidden instruction that tells Claude to skip its usual preamble. You test this and find the preamble disappears even though no such instruction is added anywhere in the request. What actually explains why prefill suppresses it?
options: The API detects the prefilled text and automatically instructs the model server-side to omit any introductory sentences it would otherwise have generated.
Prefilling forces stop_reason to resolve to stop_sequence immediately, before any preamble tokens have a chance to be generated at all.
Claude continues generating from the exact text you supplied, so a turn that already opens with a fence has no place left for a preamble sentence to go.
Prefilling strips any preamble tokens Claude generates before they are included in the returned response content sent back to the caller.
questions.explain: Prefill is continuation, not instruction: the assistant turn already begins mid-structure, so there is no sentence-starting position left for a preamble to occupy. There's no server-side detection or instruction-injection happening — the API doesn't rewrite your request based on prefilled content. stop_reason only becomes stop_sequence once generation actually reaches your stop string, which happens after the JSON, not instead of the preamble. And nothing is stripped after the fact — the model simply never produces preamble tokens because generation started somewhere past where they would go.

reviewQuestions.q: Your team wants to reuse the prefill-plus-stop-sequence technique from your JSON extraction endpoint on two new endpoints: one that returns Python code snippets, and one that returns CSV rows. A reviewer says the technique only works for JSON responses. Is the reviewer right?
options: Yes — prefill and stop sequences only work for JSON because the API validates the closing fence against the JSON Schema before returning the response.
No — the technique works for any output with an unambiguous opening and closing delimiter, so fenced code blocks and CSV rows can use the same approach as JSON.
Only partially — prefill still works for code and CSV, but a stop sequence can only be defined as a single-character delimiter like a closing brace.
No, but only for outputs whose total length is known in advance, since the stop sequence needs a fixed number of tokens to search across.
reviewQuestions.explain: The requirement is a delimiter, not a format: anything you can open with a known prefix and close with a known suffix — a code fence, a CSV header line, a closing bracket — works the same way JSON's fence does. There's no JSON Schema validation involved in stop sequences at all, so that claim invents a mechanism that isn't part of how prefill works. Stop sequences aren't limited to single characters either; they can be any string, including a full closing fence like triple backticks. And nothing about the technique depends on knowing output length ahead of time — generation simply halts whenever the stop string appears.

reviewQuestions.q: You're debugging an extraction pipeline that uses prefill plus a stop_sequence on the closing fence. A run completes normally and the returned JSON parses without error. Which stop_reason value should you expect to see in the API response for that run?
options: end_turn, because the model considers the JSON object a complete, well-formed response on its own, with nothing left to generate.
tool_use, because returning structured JSON is treated internally the same way as a tool call would be, even without a defined tool.
max_tokens, because the fence-and-stop pattern is designed to cap generation length rather than to match a specific string.
stop_sequence, because generation halted the moment the model produced the string you supplied as the stop condition.
reviewQuestions.explain: stop_sequence is reported specifically when generation halts because it matched one of the strings you passed in stop_sequences — exactly what happens when the closing fence appears. end_turn is what you'd see if the model decided on its own that the response was finished, which isn't what's driving termination here. tool_use only appears when the model actually invokes a defined tool, and no tool is involved in a prefill-based text extraction. max_tokens would indicate the response was cut off for hitting the token limit, a failure mode you want to avoid, not the expected outcome of a clean stop-sequence match.

knowledgePoints.name: The tool that is never called
knowledgePoints.teach:
For production extraction there is a sturdier option than hoping prose parses. Define a tool whose input_schema is the output contract, and read the structured input off the tool_use block:

tools = [{
  "name": "record_invoice",
  "description": "Record the fields extracted from an invoice.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invoice_number": {"type": "string"},
      "total_cents":    {"type": "integer"},
      "due_date":       {"type": "string", "format": "date"}
    },
    "required": ["invoice_number", "total_cents"]
  }
}]

There need not be a real function behind it. The tool exists so the model has a typed shape to fill, and the API validates the shape on the way out.

Prefill hopes for valid JSON. A schema asks the API to enforce it.

Use a generic to_json-style tool for a quick prototype or changing requirements; use a dedicated schema for complex, high-accuracy production work.

questions.q: Your invoice extractor currently uses prefill-and-stop-sequence and mostly works, but roughly 2% of responses still return slightly malformed JSON that fails to parse. A teammate suggests switching to a tool whose input_schema describes the invoice fields instead. What is the actual advantage of that approach for this production case?
options: Tool calls execute against a more capable internal model variant, which produces more accurate field extraction than a prefilled text response would generate.
The schema declares the output's structure, and the API validates the tool_use input against it, catching malformed shapes instead of hoping they won't occur.
Defining a tool automatically reduces the number of output tokens generated, which lowers the chance of a truncated, unparsable response overall.
Once any tool is defined for a request, prefilling the assistant turn is disabled entirely, forcing the model onto the more reliable tool-calling path.
questions.explain: A tool's input_schema is a declared contract that the API validates the tool_use input against, so a malformed shape gets caught rather than slipping through as parse-breaking text — that is the real gap prefill can't close. There's no separate, more-capable model invoked for tool calls; it's the same model responding in a different format. Defining a tool doesn't inherently shrink output token counts either — the fields still need to be generated, just as structured arguments instead of prose. And prefill isn't disabled by defining tools; the two techniques are independent, even though you'd typically pick one for a given response.

questions.q: Two teams are building extraction endpoints. Team A is prototyping a new document type and expects the fields they care about to change weekly as they learn what's useful. Team B has a stable, high-accuracy production endpoint for invoices that has been unchanged for months. Which team should reach for a generic to_json-style tool rather than a dedicated schema?
options: Team A — a generic tool suits prototyping and requirements that are still moving, while a dedicated schema fits Team B's stable, production case better.
Team B — a generic tool is best once an endpoint is stable and unchanging, since there is no further need to keep updating the schema at all.
Both teams — a generic to_json tool is strictly better in every case because it removes the maintenance burden of hand-written schemas entirely.
Neither team — generic tools should only be used when no schema validation is needed at all, which applies to neither scenario here.
questions.explain: A generic tool is the better fit exactly when requirements are still changing and speed of iteration matters more than tight validation — that's Team A's situation. Team B's endpoint is the opposite case: stable and high-accuracy, which is what a dedicated schema is suited for, so assigning the generic tool there gets it backwards. It isn't strictly better in all cases either — a dedicated schema catches malformed output more precisely, which production work benefits from. And both scenarios still want some schema validation; the choice is which shape of schema to use, not whether to validate at all.

knowledgePoints.name: Shape is not truth
knowledgePoints.teach:
A JSON Schema validates structure. It has nothing to say about whether the values are right.

The schema catchesThe schema misses
total_cents is a string, not an integertotal_cents is 1200 when the invoice says 12000
due_date is missingdue_date is in the past
an unknown field appearedinvoice_number belongs to a different customer

Validate the returned values in application code. A schema validates shape, not business truth.

This is the same boundary as everywhere else in the section: the model's output is input to your system, and input gets checked.

questions.q: An invoice's total reads $12,340.00, but your extraction tool returns a well-formed record with total_cents: 123400 — off by a factor of ten from the correct 1,234,000. The record passes schema validation without any errors. What actually failed here?
options: The input_schema, because it should have included a numeric range constraint bounding total_cents to a plausible range of invoice amounts.
The tool_choice setting, because forcing the tool only ran validation on presence and type instead of on the correctness of values.
The underlying model tier, because correctly extracting a ten-fold amount requires a larger model than the one used for this call.
Nothing at the schema level — the record was well-formed, and only application-level validation against the source would have caught the error.
questions.explain: The schema's job is to check that total_cents is present and is an integer, both of which were true here, so it passed — the error is a wrong-but-well-typed value, which only application code cross-checking the value against the source document can catch. A range constraint might rule out some implausible values but wouldn't reliably catch an off-by-ten error that's still numerically plausible for an invoice, so narrowing the schema isn't the real fix. Presence and type checks in the schema aren't tied to tool_choice, which governs whether and which tool gets called, not what gets checked inside the call. And this isn't a model-capacity problem — the failure is a missing validation step, not a math limitation of the model tier.

questions.q: You're listing out which checks belong in your invoice tool's JSON Schema versus which belong in your application's post-extraction validation code. Which of the following is actually something the JSON Schema itself checks?
options: That the extracted due_date value falls in the future relative to today's date on the calendar.
That the extracted invoice_number matches a record already stored in your customer database.
That a required field like total_cents is present in the response and typed as an integer.
That the total_cents value matches the sum of the invoice's individual line items exactly.
questions.explain: Presence and type checks are exactly what a JSON Schema is designed to enforce — required fields exist, and their values match the declared type. Whether a date is in the future, whether an identifier matches your database, and whether a total reconciles with line items are all business rules about the meaning of the values, not their shape, so none of them are things a schema checks — they belong in application-level validation instead.

reviewQuestions.q: You're defining a record_invoice tool purely so Claude has a typed shape to fill when extracting invoice data — there's no invoicing system for it to actually call. A reviewer objects that every tool definition must correspond to a real function the API will invoke server-side. Is the reviewer correct?
options: No — a tool used for structured output need not correspond to any real function; it exists only to give the model a typed shape, read off the tool_use block.
Yes — the Claude API executes the named function server-side and returns its result as part of the response, so an implementation is required for this to work.
Partially — a stub function is required, but it can simply return the same input it received without performing any real work of its own.
Yes, but only for tools with more than a handful of properties, where the API needs a real implementation to validate nested structures correctly.
reviewQuestions.explain: There need not be a real function behind a structured-output tool at all — it's a contract describing the shape you want, and your application code reads the arguments straight off the tool_use block without calling anything. The Claude API never executes functions server-side; all tool execution, if any happens, is the caller's responsibility, which rules out the idea that an implementation is required. A stub isn't needed either, since there's no dispatch step waiting to invoke one. And schema size has nothing to do with whether an implementation exists — validation of the shape happens the same way regardless of how many properties are declared.

knowledgePoints.name: Three settings, three guarantees
knowledgePoints.teach:
tool_choiceguaranteeuse when
autoClaude may call a tool, or may answer in proseClaude should judge whether the tool applies
anySome tool will be calleda tool is required, but which one is Claude's call
naming a toolThat tool will be calledstructured output is mandatory

Force the tool when the endpoint must always return a record. Leave it auto when 'no structured answer applies' is a legitimate outcome.

The failure mode of leaving it on auto for a mandatory-extraction endpoint is intermittent and unpleasant: it works on the clear cases and returns prose on exactly the ambiguous inputs where you most needed a record.

questions.q: Your extraction endpoint has two tools defined: record_invoice, which captures structured invoice fields, and flag_for_review, used for genuinely unreadable documents. The endpoint must always call record_invoice for every input — flagging is not a valid response here. With tool_choice set to auto, roughly 8% of malformed-but-readable invoices come back as a plain-text explanation instead of either tool being called. Which tool_choice setting guarantees record_invoice is the tool called every time?
options: any, so Claude is required to call some tool, whether that turns out to be record_invoice or flag_for_review, depending on the input.
auto, combined with a stronger system-prompt instruction telling Claude to always call record_invoice regardless of input quality.
auto, with a lower temperature so Claude converges more consistently on calling record_invoice instead of answering in prose.
record_invoice, named directly in tool_choice, since naming a tool is the only setting that guarantees that exact tool gets called.
questions.explain: Naming record_invoice directly is the only setting that guarantees that exact tool is what gets called, which is what this endpoint requires. any would guarantee a tool call but not which one — Claude could still call flag_for_review, which doesn't satisfy the requirement. Keeping auto and adding a stronger instruction still leaves the choice probabilistic, which is exactly the behavior producing the 8% prose responses. And temperature affects how confidently tokens are sampled; it has no effect on whether tool_choice: auto decides to invoke a tool versus answer in prose.

questions.q: You're building a research agent with three tools: search_web, search_docs, and search_code. For a general query, you want to guarantee the agent calls one of these three tools rather than answering directly from its own knowledge, but you're fine with the agent deciding which of the three is most relevant. Which tool_choice setting matches this requirement?
options: The specific tool most likely to apply, forced by name, guaranteeing that exact tool and none of the other two is ever called.
any, which guarantees some one of the three tools is called on every turn, while leaving the choice of which tool entirely to Claude.
auto, which guarantees a tool is called whenever Claude judges the query to be search-related, and prose is returned otherwise.
any, which guarantees all three tools are called in sequence so their results can be compared before Claude answers.
questions.explain: any is exactly the setting for 'a tool must be called, but which one is up to the model' — it guarantees some tool call without dictating which of the three fires. Naming one specific tool would guarantee that tool only, which is stronger than needed here and would prevent the agent from picking search_docs or search_code when either is the better fit. auto doesn't guarantee anything — it explicitly allows Claude to skip tools entirely and answer in prose, which is the outcome this requirement rules out. And any doesn't call every defined tool; it guarantees one call, not a sweep across all of them.

reviewQuestions.q: A support-ticket triage endpoint uses tool_choice: auto with a single tool, classify_ticket. In production it returns a plain-text response instead of calling the tool on roughly 1 in 20 requests, breaking the downstream router that expects a structured category every time. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Lower the temperature so Claude settles into calling classify_ticket more consistently across requests over time.
Rewrite the tool's description to more clearly explain when classify_ticket applies, while keeping tool_choice on auto.
Set tool_choice to name classify_ticket directly, since forcing it is a guarantee rather than a probabilistic nudge.
Add retry logic that resubmits the request whenever a prose response comes back, until a tool call is finally returned.
reviewQuestions.explain: Naming classify_ticket directly in tool_choice guarantees it fires on every request — the router needs a structured category every time, and that's exactly what forcing the tool provides instead of hoping for it. Lowering temperature might nudge the failure rate down but doesn't eliminate the underlying possibility of a prose response, since auto never rules that outcome out entirely. A clearer tool description can help auto perform better on average, but it's still a probabilistic improvement, not a guarantee. And retrying on prose responses adds latency and cost to paper over a problem that a single settings change removes outright.
